general_conventions: M1 = method mark; A marks dependent on it cannot be scored unless the M mark is earned. A1 = accuracy/answer mark, often awarded for a correct final answer which then implies earlier C marks.
C1 = compensatory (method) mark that can be awarded for correct working even if the final answer is wrong; a correct final answer normally earns all C marks.
B1 = independent mark, not dependent on other marks.
A0 on a show-that line means the given value earns no credit by itself; the mark is for the working shown.

ECF (error carried forward): later numerical parts can earn full credit if consistent with an earlier wrong answer; ECF is allowed after arithmetic (AE), transcription (TE) and power-of-ten (POT) errors but not after wrong physics/equation (XP).
POT: power-of-ten error, usually from SI prefix conversion; the mark where it happens is lost, then ECF applies.
TE: wrong copying of data from question, graph, booklet or earlier answer; lose that mark only, then ECF.
XP: using an incorrect equation counts as wrong physics even if it gives the right number.
SF: giving more significant figures than justified is not penalised; too few sig figs is handled within individual mark points and penalised only once in the paper.
CON: contradictory statements in one answer score no mark. BOD = benefit of the doubt.

Conventions: '/' separates alternative acceptable answers; Reject/Not = not creditworthy; Ignore = irrelevant; Allow = acceptable; words in brackets are not essential; underlined words must appear; AW = alternative wording; ORA = or reverse argument.

Level of Response (6-mark, asterisked) questions are marked holistically: decide the level from the science and the quality of reasoning, then the higher/lower mark within the level by communication. L1 = 1-2, L2 = 3-4, L3 = 5-6 marks; L1^/L2^/L3^ annotate the lower mark in each level.

LoR communication strands: L3 needs a well-developed line of reasoning, clear and logically structured, relevant and substantiated; L2 a line of reasoning with some structure, mostly relevant, supported by some evidence; L1 basic, unstructured information with limited evidence; 0 = nothing worthy of credit.
Alternative correct approaches and unexpected methods must be credited fairly.

MACB categorisation: B marks must be specifically seen; M marks must be seen and gate dependent A marks; C marks can be implied by later correct working (e.g. a correct substitution implies knowledge of the equation); A marks depend on an M mark or allow C marks to be scored.
Significant figures rule: if data are given to 2 s.f., answers to 2 or more s.f. are allowed; fewer than 2 s.f. is penalised once only in the whole paper unless additional guidance says otherwise.
For substitution into an equation any rearranged subject is allowed unless guidance says otherwise.
Crossed-out work is not marked if a clear alternative is given; contradictory responses score nothing even if one part is correct.
List questions: only the required number of responses are marked, left to right then line by line; extra responses hedging bets gain no credit.
LoR marking: read the whole answer, use a best-fit approach; the science content sets the level and the communication statement (in italics) decides the higher or lower mark within the level.
NR is used when nothing is written; 0 is given for written work not worthy of credit (including copying the question).
Levels of response questions on this paper are 3 and 8.

questions.context: Describe measuring h and t; use t vs √h graph to find g with % uncertainty.
questions.answer: Gradient ≈ 0.44-0.47 s m^-1/2 = √(2/g), g ≈ 9.5 m s^-2; % uncertainty in g = 2 × % in gradient
marking_points: L3 (5-6): clear method to measure h and t and graph analysed to give g and its percentage uncertainty
L2 (3-4): some method and attempted analysis for g and uncertainty; OR clear method with limited analysis; OR limited method with full analysis
L1 (1-2): limited method for h or t OR limited analysis for g

Indicative (method): metre rule/tape (not ruler) clamped vertically; set square/fiducial marker; timer linked to electromagnet and trapdoor; switching off magnet starts timer, ball hitting trapdoor stops it; allow for ball diameter in h; resolution mm and ms (light gates/video ignored)

Indicative (analysis): gradient = √(2/g) so g = 2/gradient²; method for gradient; gradient 0.44-0.47; g ≈ 9.5 m s^-2 with correct power of ten and unit; worst acceptable line and its gradient; absolute and % uncertainty in gradient; % uncertainty in g = 2 × % uncertainty in gradient or from worst g values

questions.subtopic: electron diffraction and de Broglie wavelength comparison
questions.context: Describe safe electron diffraction experiment, how it shows wave nature, and compare λ for electrons vs a car at 110 km/h.
questions.answer: Rings from diffraction by graphite atom spacing, λ_e ≈ 10^-10 m; car λ ≈ 10^-38 m, so λ_e >> λ_car
marking_points: L3 (5-6): clear description of experiment and observations and detailed comparison of de Broglie wavelengths
L2 (3-4): some description and some comparison; OR limited description with detailed comparison; OR clear description with limited comparison
L1 (1-2): limited description of experiment and observations OR attempt at the car's de Broglie wavelength

Indicative (experiment): electrons accelerated by high p.d. in vacuum; fired at graphite target; rings observed (diagram of apparatus/rings); diffraction by atomic spacing so λ ≈ spacing; higher p.d. gives smaller rings; many layers/orientations so diffraction in all directions gives rings; safety: avoid touching high-voltage terminals, insulated leads
Indicative (comparison): λ_electron ≈ 10^-10 m; λ = h/p; car mass estimate 500-3000 kg; speed 30.5-30.6 m s^-1; λ_car ≈ 7 × 10^-39 to 4 × 10^-38 m; λ_electron >> λ_car
